name: discord-ops
desc: 6-agent Claude council fronted by Discord. Multi-model fallback via a sandboxed Codex bridge, admin elevation broker, cron scheduler, voice notes, vault write-guard.

detail.sub: A Discord-fronted Claude Agent SDK council. An operator agent coordinates a set of specialists plus per-thread sub-agents, with a GPT-5.5 fallback path over a sandboxed Codex bridge. FastAPI + SQLite, admin-elevation broker, cron scheduler, ElevenLabs voice notes, vault write-guard hook.
paragraphs: discord-ops is the personal-instance production system that Domo graduated out of. An operator agent coordinates a small council via Discord DMs and a dedicated channel, spawns per-thread sub-agents for isolated work, and exposes a local Mission Control dashboard for status + intervention. It runs on the same second-brain vault as shared memory.

The interesting parts aren't the agents themselves — those are off-the-shelf Claude. The interesting parts are the seam, the scheduler, and the broker: a per-feature wire pattern that scopes tools per-agent and self-disables when config is absent; a cron runner that's safe to retry; and a Windows admin-elevation broker that passes only an approved request token over a local channel (never the command text itself).

Recent additions push past a single vendor: a GPT-5.5 specialist over a sandboxed Codex CLI bridge backs the council — scheduled pipelines run server-side on it and fall back to the Claude agent automatically — and a separated GPT-5 evaluator grades the nightly research brief, so the generator never grades its own work. Mornings, the 7AM scan ends with an ElevenLabs voice note: a ~60-second spoken summary played live in a voice channel and attached as an mp3.

paragraphs: One Windows service hosts the Discord bot. Every inbound message passes a single-user auth gate at receipt — before any LLM call — then dispatches to a persistent runner per agent. Tool calls route through the Claude Agent SDK to in-process MCP servers, and every invocation crosses a PreToolUse policy hook, even under bypassPermissions. High-trust execution lives in a separate elevated service the bot can only reach by request token.

Every feature wires through the same seam: a per-feature pattern that scopes tools per agent and self-disables when its config is absent. That one convention is why the public Domo build runs with zero personal data — strip the config, and the feature folds away cleanly.

paragraphs: The reliability layer is boring on purpose. NSSM supervises the bot service; a SYSTEM-level watchdog re-checks it on a timer; boot recovery gates on DNS before starting; scheduled jobs are idempotent and safe to retry. None of it is exotic — all of it is measured.

Liveness is measured, not assumed: satellite clients beacon heartbeats into health tables, a stale heartbeat posts exactly one alert, and recovery posts the all-clear. The feed on the homepage is the public slice — GitHub events, sanitized server-side before the browser ever sees them.

The production repo is private, but the architecture is public twice over: the MIT-licensed Domo extraction carries the full structure, and the load-bearing internals are quoted below exactly as they appear in source.

snippets.title: // ELEVATION BROKER · WIRE PROTOCOL
snippets.caption: The payload over the pipe is only a UUID. The broker re-reads the approved command from its own store, re-hashes it, compares, then executes — the bot can't lie over the pipe to bypass approval.

snippets.title: // PRETOOLUSE GUARD · WHY THERE IS NO VERB ALLOWLIST
snippets.code:
# Read/exfil verbs are open-ended (cat, head, sed, awk, cp, scp,
# dd, xxd, base64, python -c, ruby -e, perl, ...). Listing "all" is
# impossible; verb-based gating fails open under adversarial framing.
snippets.caption: Any shell command that mentions a sensitive filename is denied, whatever verb wraps it. False positives are accepted; an entire class of bypass is closed.

files.note: MIT extraction — council, Mission Control, cron, elevation, plugin seam

paragraphs: The agents have real tools — email, calendar, elevated PowerShell, a knowledge vault — so the threat model is the architecture. The full write-up maps every control onto the OWASP LLM Top 10 (2025), including an explicit list of what the model does not defend against.

controls.name: Capability minimization
controls.desc: Per-agent MCP allowlists; an injected instruction can't invoke a tool the agent doesn't have. The persona can be jailbroken; the allowlist cannot.

controls.name: HITL approval embeds
controls.desc: Irreversible tools block on a Discord Approve/Deny; resolved embeds are edited in place so the audit trail is the message itself.

controls.name: Privilege separation
controls.desc: Elevated execution in a separate LocalSystem service; UUID-only payloads; non-overridable deny list requiring a code change to alter.

controls.name: PreToolUse fences
controls.desc: Filename-first denial of secret reads and protected writes — raw/ sources, persona files, and bot source are read-only even in autonomous mode.

controls.name: Single-user auth gate
controls.desc: Messages from anyone but the operator drop at receipt, before any LLM call — the cheapest control absorbs the cheapest attack.

name: Domo
desc: Standalone public release of the platform. Sanitized extraction with plugin seam and wizard installer.

detail.sub: The MIT-licensed public extraction of discord-ops. Personal subsystems are excluded; the multi-agent core, Mission Control dashboard, cron, calendar, video, GPT-5 bridge, and admin elevation ship behind a plugin seam with a setup wizard.
paragraphs: Domo is the sanitized, open-source version of the private discord-ops bot. It keeps the architecture — operator + specialist council, per-thread sub-agents, Mission Control dashboard, cron scheduler, calendar, video/watch, a GPT-5 specialist bridge, admin elevation, a credit governor, and a vault write-guard — and strips everything personal.

The point of Domo is the plugin seam: every feature wires through a single pattern that scopes tools per-agent and self-disables when its config is absent, so the public build runs with zero personal data and an installer wizard provisions the rest.

name: second-brain
desc: Living knowledge vault — read-only raw/ sources curated into an atomic, linked wiki/. Shared agent memory.

detail.sub: A Karpathy-pattern personal knowledge vault: a read-only raw/ of source material (exports, transcripts, articles) curated by Claude into an atomic, source-attributed, [[wiki-linked]] wiki/. The shared memory layer the agents read and write.
paragraphs: second-brain separates raw/ (never modified — exports, transcripts, articles, notes) from wiki/ (Claude-maintained atomic pages with required frontmatter and inline source attribution). Slash skills (/ingest, /lint, /log, /standup, /query) maintain the structure and keep it healthy.
The design goal is contextual memory, mistake-tracking, and progress documentation — every page links back to prior work and flags what previously failed and why.

name: elevation-broker
desc: Privilege-separation service. The bot requests approved Windows admin ops via token only — never command text.

detail.sub: A two-service privilege-separation design. The bot runs as the user; a separate broker runs elevated and accepts only an approved request token over a local channel — so the bot can trigger approved admin operations without ever holding elevated rights itself.
paragraphs: The elevation-broker exists so the assistant can perform approved Windows administrative actions without escalating its own privileges. The main bot runs unprivileged; the broker runs elevated and only ever receives an opaque request token over a local channel — never the command string.
Every elevated action is gated behind an explicit Discord Approve/Deny step, so privilege use is auditable and human-approved rather than implicit.

featureList.desc: Unprivileged bot + elevated broker; no shared privilege.

featureList.name: Token-only payload
featureList.desc: The broker validates a request token, not arbitrary command text.

featureList.desc: Each elevated op requires an explicit human Approve/Deny.

name: home-server
desc: Self-hosted bare-metal Windows box running the agent service, scheduled jobs, and secure remote access.

detail.sub: The bare-metal Windows host the agent stack runs on. NSSM keeps the bot alive as a service; Task Scheduler drives nightly jobs; Tailscale provides secure remote access. Migrated off a hypervisor to bare metal for reliability.
paragraphs: home-server is the reliability layer under everything else: a self-hosted Windows machine that runs the agent service via NSSM, executes scheduled jobs through Task Scheduler, and is reachable only over a private Tailscale mesh.

It was deliberately migrated from a hypervisor to bare metal to cut a layer of failure and simplify recovery — the operational-reliability discipline from service-desk work applied to a personal stack.

name: email-cull
desc: Daily Gmail triage pipeline — scan, propose, human-approve, apply. HMAC-gated, idempotent, vault-logged.

detail.sub: A daily inbox-cleanup pipeline. It scans Gmail against rules, proposes cull candidates, waits for human approval in Mission Control, then a separate subprocess applies the change. State-machine per scan, HMAC-signed thread tokens, idempotent retries.
paragraphs: email-cull is a safety-first automation: it never trashes anything on its own. A scan proposes candidates, the operator approves them in the dashboard, and only then does an isolated apply step act — each thread referenced by an HMAC-signed token so a stale or forged reference can't act.
It's built as a state machine per scan with pre-flight guards, stale-thread detection, and idempotent retries — the same correctness discipline as production service work, applied to an inbox.

featureList.desc: Three stages; nothing is trashed without explicit approval.

featureList.name: HMAC-signed tokens
featureList.desc: Every thread reference is signed; stale/forged refs are rejected.

featureList.desc: Retries are safe; pre-flight guards + stale-thread detection.

name: email-triage-ts
desc: NestJS + TypeScript + DynamoDB port of the email-cull pipeline, with a React operator dashboard and an eval-gated LLM spam scorer.

detail.sub: A sanitized TypeScript port of the private email-cull pipeline: scheduled scanner proposes, a human approves per-thread, a separate worker applies — re-expressed as NestJS modules over single-table DynamoDB, with a same-origin React/Vite operator dashboard and an LLM spam scorer behind a CI-gated evaluation harness.
paragraphs: email-triage-ts is the public, fictional-data port of the private email-cull subsystem — the same design instincts on a NestJS / AWS stack. SQLite's guarded transactions become DynamoDB conditional writes: every status transition is an UpdateItem with a ConditionExpression, and a failed compare-and-set maps to HTTP 409. The HMAC opaque-token boundary survives the port bit-for-bit — a frozen vector generated by the original Python codec is asserted in CI.

The scanner scores each thread with an LLM behind a typed, eval-gated port. Four scorers (schema validation, exact-match precision/recall, numeric tolerance, LLM-as-judge) run keyless in CI against committed gold; the harness drove a real prompt iteration on record, lifting recall 0.45 → 0.75 with precision holding at 0.94. A React/Vite operator dashboard is served same-origin by the API, so the live SSE ledger is a plain EventSource.

featureList.desc: Every transition is a DynamoDB compare-and-set; a racing worker can't double-finalize.

featureList.name: Out-of-process apply + reconciliation
featureList.desc: Crash-isolated worker streams JSONL; on any exit the API re-reads and heals the scan.

paragraphs: A NestJS modular monolith with hexagonal seams: GmailPort, SpamScorer, and ApplyRunner are interfaces. The fixture adapters that keep the test suite hermetic and the Fargate apply-worker planned for Phase 2 are both just adapters — no controller-layer change either way.

State lives in single-table DynamoDB with a sparse GSI. Every status transition is a conditional write; a failed compare-and-set maps to HTTP 409. The apply worker runs out of process and streams JSONL events — if it dies mid-flight, the API reconciles the scan from terminal markers rather than trusting the worker's last word.

name: voice-bridge
desc: MacBook → Windows voice dictation over RDP. Hold a hotkey, speak, release — cleaned text lands in the focused Windows app in ~2s.

detail.sub: A personal dictation bridge: a Mac client captures mic audio behind a global hotkey (Quartz event tap, so the key never leaks into RDP), ships it to a Windows-side sidecar, transcribes via Whisper, and pastes the cleaned text into the foreground app — clipboard + Ctrl+V primary, per-character SendInput fallback.
paragraphs: The hard parts are all at the edges. On the Mac, a Quartz CGEventTap consumes exactly one key (Right Option) so the push-to-talk hotkey never reaches the RDP session — the naive global-listener approach swallows the entire keyboard. On Windows, pasting into an RDP session is its own discipline: a clipboard + Ctrl+V primary path with the prior clipboard saved and restored, and a per-character SendInput fallback for when another process holds the clipboard lock.

It runs as a session-bound sidecar under Task Scheduler with layered durability: a 1-minute self-heal trigger, restart-on-failure, an RDP-reconnect trigger, launchd KeepAlive on the Mac, and a beacon heartbeat from the Mac client into a health table that arms a down-alert when the heartbeat goes stale. That hardening was earned: a heap-corruption crash the process could not catch was traced to a background clipboard restore racing the RDP clipboard agent — the full write-up is in Writing.
